newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Khmer Rouge rebels turn to politics from genocide.
newsitem.headline: Khmer Rouge rebels turn to politics from genocide.

text.p: Khmer Rouge guerrillas, who starved, tortured or worked to death more than a million Cambodians during their "killing fields" regime, are now turning to politics in a bid to survive, analysts said on Thursday.

They said a wave of more than 12,000 defections over the past week has stripped the Khmer Rouge of its might and left only 800 to 2,000 fighters concentrated in the hardline base of Anlong Veng near Thailand.
Most of the defectors, exchanging Mao caps for army uniforms, saw politics as their last chance of power.

"They are looking for legitimacy," said parliamentarian Ahmad Yahya of the most high-profile defectors, those loyal to Ieng Sary and who broke with hardliners in August to form the Democratic National United Movement (DNUM).
DNUM fighters merged with government forces this week.
"If the (DNUM) can form a party...and get one seat in the National Assembly, the Khmer Rouge will survive forever," he said.
"The military operations are over," said one Western military analyst. "Politics are what is important now."

Ieng Sary's faction, which has merged forces with the government, has maintained neutrality, which could be used as a bargaining tool as the 1998 elections approach and the co-premiers seek allies, analysts said.
The coalition's first co-premier is Prince Norodom Ranariddh, from the royalist FUNCINPEC, while second co-premier Hun Sen represents the Cambodian People's Party, the former communist power.

"I stand in the middle. I don't join either FUNCINPEC or the Cambodian People's Party," Ieng Sary, foreign minister to the notorious Pol Pot during the Khmer Rouge's 1975-79 rule, said upon merging his Pailin forces with the government troops last Wednesday.
Ieng Sary has claimed more than 20,000 followers, including families of cadres, and how they and the tens of thousands of other defector families vote is of concern to politicians.
A Western military analyst said the Khmer Rouge defectors may have lost their war, but negotiations with the government had given them political bargaining power.
"The Khmer Rouge ideology is finished. But they can still play a role because of rivalries within the FUNCINPEC and Cambodian People's Party," the analyst said.
The unravelling of the Khmer Rouge, whose ideology was based on radical agrarian reform, has driven deep rifts between the co-premiers as each has wooed defectors to his side.

"It is a big competition. Each party wants to reinforce its own forces and claim the moral achievement of winning peace for Cambodia," said the analyst, noting Hun Sen scored a coup in the past week with the lion's share of defectors going to his party.
The defectors' entry into politics has sparked anger as well as confusion over which way they will vote.
"It would be outrageous to have those people to be part of the leadership of the Cambodian nation," said Lao Mong Hay, executive director of the Khmer Institute of Democracy.
"In Cambodia, anything is possible...but we would fight that prospect," he said.
Hun Sen predicted early this week the group would be finished as a military power by mid-1997.

The 1975-1979 regime left more than one million Cambodians dead from murder, malnutrition, overwork and disease, and the guerrillas have fought the government since being ousted from power by the Vietnamese in 1979.
The Maoist group reneged on a 1991 U.N.-sponsored peace pact, continuing to fight the coalition government elected in 1993.
"They will disintegrate slowly," one analyst said. "Maybe in 10 years they will have 100 men in the jungle. But like everyone (wanted), the Khmer Rouge fighters will fade away."
